source.title: Attentional Focus and Cueing for Speed Development

paper.citation: Winkelman, N. C. (2018). Attentional focus and cueing for speed development. Strength & Conditioning Journal, 40(1), 13–25. https://doi.org/10.1519/SSC.0000000000000266
paper.abstract: How can attentional-focus research and sprint biomechanics inform coaching instruction and cue selection for acceleration and maximal-velocity development? This is an applied narrative article, not a new participant study. The cited attentional-focus studies span novice, intermediate, and expert participants and multiple tasks; the directly discussed sprint evidence includes block-start sprinters, novices, and nine trained collegiate football players. The framework concerns motor-skill instruction and does not address physical-capacity programming or injury treatment. Narrative synthesis and practitioner framework integrating attentional-focus, motor-learning, and sprint-biomechanics literature. No systematic search, eligibility criteria, study-quality assessment, or quantitative synthesis is reported, so completeness and selection bias cannot be evaluated from the article. The author organizes external-focus cues by distance, direction, and descriptive language and then maps examples to acceleration and maximal-velocity mechanics.
paper.tldr: This applied narrative review offers a practical framework for designing sprint cues while illustrating where attentional-focus evidence is stronger, mixed, or extrapolated. In one cited 10-m sprint experiment, an external-focus condition produced faster total, reaction, and running times than an internal-focus condition. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Narrative synthesis and practitioner framework integrating attentional-focus, motor-learning, and sprint-biomechanics literature. No systematic search, eligibility criteria, study-quality assessment, or quantitative synthesis is reported, so completeness and selection bias cannot be evaluated from the article. The author organizes external-focus cues by distance, direction, and descriptive language and then maps examples to acceleration and maximal-velocity mechanics.
paper.findings: In one cited 10-m sprint experiment, an external-focus condition produced faster total, reaction, and running times than an internal-focus condition. Cited novice data favored an external focus over internal and control cues for 20-m sprinting, whereas trained collegiate football players showed no difference for 0–10 or 0–20 yards and performed better under control instructions for the 10–20-yard split. The paper therefore documents skill- and context-dependent findings rather than uniform superiority of external cues across all sprint tasks and athlete experience levels. The proposed framework emphasizes identifying the athlete's primary coordinative limitation, then individualizing an external cue through distance, direction, and description.
paper.limitations: This is a non-systematic narrative review; its recommendations should not be treated as pooled causal estimates. Several cited sprint studies used cues containing more than one focus point, complicating attribution of effects to internal versus external focus. The direction element of the framework is partly reinterpreted from jumping studies rather than directly tested in sprint cueing. The article explicitly notes that cueing is unlikely to correct a primary limitation in strength or another physical quality until that underlying issue is addressed. Acute performance changes do not necessarily demonstrate retention, transfer, or long-term speed development.
paper.practicalImplications: Prefer short, outcome-oriented cues as a starting point, then test them athlete by athlete and task by task. Evaluate whether a cue improves the intended movement without degrading timing or output, and reassess at later sessions to distinguish immediate compliance from learning. When the constraint is physical capacity rather than coordination, change the training problem rather than adding more words.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete development, prefer short, outcome-oriented cues as a starting point, then test them athlete by athlete and task by task. Evaluate whether a cue improves the intended movement without degrading timing or output, and reassess at later sessions to distinguish immediate compliance from learning. When the constraint is physical capacity rather than coordination, change the training problem rather than adding more words. Preserve the study population and avoid converting one finding into a universal development pathway or benchmark.
paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, prefer short, outcome-oriented cues as a starting point, then test them athlete by athlete and task by task. Evaluate whether a cue improves the intended movement without degrading timing or output, and reassess at later sessions to distinguish immediate compliance from learning. When the constraint is physical capacity rather than coordination, change the training problem rather than adding more words. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
